findings.issue: Documentation inaccuracy, not a code defect. The software-engineer's proveFail[1] claims that deleting the line `if (expectedOrigin === null) return null;` alone turned 'absolute URL when no app origin can be determined' red. It does NOT — I reproduced this: with only that line removed, the test still passes, because control falls through to `url.origin !== expectedOrigin` where expectedOrigin is null and url.origin is always a non-null string, so the comparison is always true and still returns null. The line is redundant defense-in-depth (it saves a URL construction and reads clearly), not the sole enforcer. Fail-closed behavior IS genuinely enforced (I confirmed the null-origin assertion goes red only when the origin COMPARISON is removed). No action needed on the code; flagging so the reviewer does not treat the SE's proveFail narrative as literally accurate.

learnings.insight: A prove-it-fails experiment must remove the line that ACTUALLY enforces the behavior, not a redundant guard that sits in front of it. Here the software-engineer attributed the null-origin fail-closed to `if (expectedOrigin === null) return null;`, but that line is redundant: the downstream `url.origin !== expectedOrigin` also rejects when expectedOrigin is null (a URL origin is always a non-null string). Deleting the redundant guard leaves the suite green, which would falsely 'prove' the test is tautological. When two guards backstop the same behavior, isolate each — a green result on removing one only means it wasn't load-bearing for that assertion, not that the assertion is worthless.
learnings.action: When a proveFail leaves the suite green, check for a second guard covering the same case before concluding the test is tautological; remove all backstops to find the true enforcer.

learnings.insight: The browser default-origin path of a validator (window.location.origin) is the code path that ACTUALLY ships when the only caller uses the default parameter, yet a node-environment suite never exercises it. It can be covered in the node environment (no happy-dom needed) with vi.stubGlobal('window', { location: { origin } }) when the origin resolver is invoked per-call (default-parameter evaluation), plus vi.unstubAllGlobals() in afterEach. This is more deterministic than happy-dom (which fixes the origin and computes no layout) and let me assert same-origin accept, cross-origin reject, and the opaque/empty fail-closed edges the injected-param tests can't reach.
learnings.action: For a pure validator whose production caller relies on an ambient default (origin/clock/locale), add at least one test that exercises the default resolver by stubbing the ambient global, not only the injected-parameter path.
